accepted.reason: Observation-target alignment is good: delayed_I is explicitly recommended for hospitalization-rate semantics and avoids introducing an explicit H compartment that may be weakly identifiable in a short single-season series. SEIRS can flexibly accommodate sharp peakiness and potential post-peak dynamics without changing the observation channel. Main risk is added waning parameter(s) that may be under-identified over 31 training weeks, but this is still a reasonable primary candidate given the series is high-peakiness and high-scale.

Good alignment via delayed_I and lower complexity than SEIRS, reducing identifiability risk for short single-season data. Serves as a parsimonious comparator to test whether waning is actually needed to represent peakiness, without changing observation semantics.

Useful control for whether an explicit delay is necessary versus being absorbed by E/I timescales. However, given the mechanistic note that admissions may lag infections, delay_weeks=0 is less plausible a priori and may force compensatory parameter distortions (timing absorbed into E/I durations), increasing interpretability/identifiability concerns.

Covers plausible 1–2 week lag at weekly resolution and maintains good observation-target alignment. Identifiability risk remains because delay can trade off with E/I durations; with high peakiness, a 2-week lag may also smear timing, but it is still a reasonable sensitivity candidate.

rejected.reason: Observation-target alignment is potentially problematic: observing H (a stock/compartment level) is not the same as weekly hospitalization admissions/rate unless the model’s H state is explicitly defined as an admission flow proxy. Additionally, adding an H compartment increases complexity and is specifically flagged as weakly identifiable for short single-season series; delayed_I is more plausible here given the surveillance semantics and limited data length.

suggested_edits.edit: Clarify that delayed_I is intended to proxy weekly admissions (rate) via a proportionality/scale parameter, and keep waning parameterization minimal to reduce identifiability risk (avoid extra waning-related degrees of freedom beyond a single return-to-S mechanism).

Note explicitly that delay_weeks=2 is a sensitivity check and may be partially non-identifiable versus E/I durations; consider constraining E/I timescales (conceptually) to avoid the delay absorbing all timing variation.

If retained later, ensure the observation map corresponds to an admission-rate-consistent quantity (e.g., an inflow to H) rather than the H stock; otherwise the mapping is misaligned with a weekly hospitalization rate target.
